title: Pretty good, one big pitfall
text:
I appreciate that this app is streamlined, and easy to use. It would be great if it tracked fat as a macro.

One thing to watch out for is the  “Recent Meals” feature on food tracking. Understand that it is not just a list of foods in standard serving sizes, but macros for the food in the quantity you last recorded. 

For example, you search the database and find the information for one cup of whole milk. But you drink a half a cup of milk and so record .5 servings. Now the .5 servings is the nutritional information stored in “Recent Meals.” 

The next time you pull whole milk off “Recent Meals” for a new diary entry it will pull that half cup “meal” up and show it as one serving. If you assume, as I did, that was indicating the standard serving from the nutritional database (1 cup) you will be off by 50%.

What would be more useful, in my opinion, is
Quick access to “Recent FOODS,” with the macros corresponding to a standard serving size that is easy to see: “Whole Milk, 1c.” 

The way it is now you have to look up everything every time, which is a drag.

Example: tried to use entry for tilapia filets, 1 is 90 calories, 20g protein. I had 2 filets so adjusted the quantity to 2, so it should read 180 / 40, but it said 360 / 80. If the app can’t do simple math multiplying calories x 2, then how can I trust it with my medical information like shot dosages, weight calculation, percentages, etc.?

Also, if you enter your meal entries out of chronological order, it saves them in the order you entered them - it doesn’t arrange them by time.

For $40 a year, not worth it. I can pay less to get features that don’t require all the manual work or just use a food logging app with an easier interface.

title: 0.5/5 — Oura Ring 4: Not worth the money
text:
Here’s my experience with the Oura Ring 4, and why I’m giving it half a star out of five.
1. Constantly inaccurate activity tracking. I can stand still or walk around my desk at work, and the ring will label it as walking or even cycling. But when I actually go for a walk, it sometimes fails to recognize it altogether.
2. Unreliable exercise detection. Even when I’m genuinely running or walking briskly, the ring detects my activity inconsistently. Sometimes it works, sometimes it doesn’t.
3. Completely ridiculous activity detection. I can be sitting in my gaming chair playing video games, and Oura will log cycling as an activity. How does that even make sense?
4. Terrible sleep tracking. In my experience, sleep tracking has become significantly worse over time. It feels like a previous update broke something, because now the ring sometimes underestimates my sleep by as much as two hours. I no longer trust its results.
On another occasion, I went on a four-hour walk with my phone, but without my Apple Watch. Oura failed to track my route entirely. I had my phone with me, yet there was no route recorded.
5. No Ukrainian or Russian language support. For a product with such an expensive subscription, the lack of basic language options is disappointing. At the very least, Ukrainian should be available. Translating an interface should not be an unreasonable expectation for a company charging customers this much.
Overall, this feels like a cash grab rather than a reliable health-tracking product. The hardware and subscription cost are simply not justified by my experience with the app. The tracking feels more like guesswork than actual measurement, and I struggle to see any meaningful benefit from using this device anymore.
What frustrates me most is that the ring seemed to work better in the past, but now I barely get any useful information from it. Instead of improving the experience and addressing these issues, the developers seem content to charge premium prices for an increasingly unreliable product.
I genuinely regret spending money on this. I cannot recommend the Oura Ring 4 in its current state.

title: Disappointing Experience With Noom Med’s Prescription Coordination
text:
I’m extremely disappointed with my experience with Noom Med. I paid $387 for the 12-week branded GLP-1 telehealth program, in addition to paying $349 separately to NovoCare for my Wegovy medication. Unfortunately, when I needed help with my prescription, the service fell short of what I expected.

My prescribing doctor messaged me confirming that my prescription had been sent. I relied on that confirmation and waited, only to contact NovoCare myself and discover that the prescription had never actually been sent.

I then reached out to Noom’s care coordination team for help. Instead of investigating the issue and helping resolve it, I was told to contact NovoCare myself. Since then, I’ve repeatedly followed up and have essentially been told to wait, with no meaningful resolution or clear timeline.

The most frustrating part is that I had to discover the problem myself after being given incorrect information, and then had to chase down the very service I’m paying for to get answers.

I understand that delays happen, but there is a difference between an unavoidable delay and being told something has been done when it hasn’t. When a service involves prescription management, communication and accountability matter.

At this point, I’ve lost confidence in Noom Med’s ability to provide reliable care coordination. I’ve requested a refund or other appropriate compensation for this service failure, but I’m still waiting for a satisfactory response.

If I’m paying $387 for telehealth support, I expect more than being told to wait and figure things out myself. I hope Noom improves its communication, accountability, and customer support for patients who depend on this service.

title: Disappointed
text:
“Psychology based” so long as your answers to quizzes fit the ones they provide, I guess.

I am currently at a fairly healthy weight, but I’m struggling with an impulse control issue. Given that Noom talks about using psychology to address eating patterns, I figured I’d give it a try. I deleted it before the free trial period ended. 

First, it threw me off to be offered probiotics before the app knew anything about me. I guess it just assumes everyone should be buying that product. I don’t need it, so it felt like a profit center more than sound nutritional advice. 

The bigger issue was that the app didn’t give me the opportunity to adequately explain my situation. My impulse control issue is related to ADHD. I’ve always struggled with it, but I was just diagnosed as having ADHD about 18 months ago. Unfortunately, I’m allergic to the stimulants that best treat ADHD. I’m currently on a non-stimulant prescription. It’s nowhere near as effective, and I’m back to having frequent evening binge eating sessions. I was hopeful Noom would help me address this behavior and give me workable solutions. 
The first issue came up with the quizzes. I encountered questions for which none of the given answers were even close, and there was no option to choose “other” or to write my own answer. 
I tried to use the help function. I got the AI bot. It asked me to upload a screenshot. I am a competent iPhone user, and I could not find a way to upload a screenshot. The bot told me it would connect me with a coach. I waited several minutes. I then replied “I can’t keep waiting on a response as I have other things I need to do.” 
I tried again, but I ran into the same issue with quizzes. Same runaround with the bot. 
Several days later, I found a bunch of emails in my junk mail folder. Tech support had contacted me by email. I didn’t know they had, so I didn’t go looking for an email. 
I replied even though I’d already deleted the app. I explained my situation with the quiz answers that are available didn’t match my situation at all, and that the bot wanted me to upload a screenshot but I couldn’t see how to do it. They replied, telling me that sounded like something that needed to be addressed by a coach… 
I imagine the stock answers the app allows a user to choose work for the majority of people. I’m not one of them, though.

The AI generated help was also pretty awful, basically saying my weight loss plateau was because I’m not eating enough “green” foods and that I should incorporate them in my diet. Unless you want to eat like a rabbit living off of spinach and arugula, anyone with a working body and a brain would know that’s impossible on a nutrition standpoint. Coaches were also super unhelpful not giving specific help on the questions you had. Most of the time, it sounded just as bad as the AI help or even worse like they’re just reading from a prompt. So if you want to spend money to obsess over food in an unhealthy manner, get advice that somehow is even worse than ChatGPT, and basically get the marketing that “oh this app is so good…..if you join our medication program!” then be my guest to spend an ungodly amount of money for the most terrible food tracking app I’ve ever used. text:

Another point of annoyance- the inability to scan labels when  adding recipe ingredients. Scanning is available for logging. Why not for recipe building? 

After briefly trying Noom Med twice (under a different account), and being assigned two different coaches, there was a glaring difference: one coach reached out often. The other didn’t reach out for 10 days. Inconsistency for this feature was glaring. 

Food color look up: You can scan a barcode or type in a food and see the same food entered as every color. It’s frustrating and not helpful. 

Price: each time I have been on Noom, pricing is always inconsistent. Sometimes I’m charged monthly, sometimes several months all at once. Sometimes there are discounted pricing, sometimes not. When canceling, I’ve been offered a lower rate to stay— why not offer the lower rate to begin with?

title: I love this app, just have a few things I wish could be added
text:
I’ve been a MyFitnessPal Premium member for about three months now, and during that time, I’ve lost 30 pounds! This app has genuinely been a huge part of my weight loss journey, and I can’t recommend it enough. There are so many useful features, the interface looks great, and everything feels intuitive and easy to navigate. It’s made tracking my nutrition and staying consistent with my goals so much easier.

That being said, there are a few features I’d love to see added or improved that I think would make an already great app even better.

1. Automatic Fasting Tracker

I really like having the fasting tracker built into the app, but I wish there were an option to have it start automatically at a scheduled time. I often forget to manually turn it on, even though I’m still following my fasting schedule. It would be great if users could set their preferred fasting window and have the timer start automatically, with the option to end the fast manually when they eat their first meal. This would make the feature much more convenient and help ensure fasting data stays accurate, even when someone forgets to start the timer.

2. More Customization for the Home Screen

One of my favorite things about the app is how easily I can see my calorie and macronutrient goals. However, I’d love to have more control over which widgets and nutritional information appear on my home screen.

For example, it would be amazing to add widgets displaying daily fiber, sodium, sugar, cholesterol, or vitamin and mineral intake. Everyone has different nutritional priorities, and being able to customize the dashboard to reflect those priorities would be incredibly useful. Ideally, users could add, remove, resize, and rearrange widgets to create a home screen tailored to their individual goals.

3. Better Long-Term Nutrition Tracking and Visualization

This is probably the feature I’d be most excited to see implemented. I love how the app allows you to visualize your weight progress over weeks, months, and longer periods. I wish that same functionality existed for calories, macronutrients, and other nutritional data.

Currently, it’s much easier to review short-term nutrition trends than to get a comprehensive picture of how your eating habits have evolved over time. I’d love to be able to select a nutrient and view its daily or average intake over the past month, three months, six months, or even a year.

For example, it would be incredibly helpful to see how my average daily protein intake has changed over the last three months, whether I’ve consistently met my fiber goals, or how my calorie intake has fluctuated throughout my weight loss journey. Having customizable graphs, moving averages, and comparisons against personal goals would make this even better.

I think this would be especially valuable for people who use the app for long-term weight management, athletic performance, or improving their overall nutrition rather than simply counting calories.

title: This WAS a good app
text:
I have been using this App for years. At the beginning it helped me through my weight-loss journey, and it was fantastic. I attributed my success, in part, to this app. Since then it has helped me maintain a healthy weight, and improve my macros intake in order to get a balanced diet and achieve better results from my training. 

Then Under Armour bought the app. This is when it went downhill. Since that time, every new update is worse than the previous one. It has come to the point that the app quits abruptly, takes the longest time to add foods, wrongly calculates your calories consumed/remaining (or takes a long time to update them after inputting foods), and worst of all, it drains my phone’s battery like crazy. I used the app for 35 sec, which only gave me time to input 2 items, and battery went from 82% to 76%. As soon as I closed the app the battery drain stopped (I have downloaded videos and articles over the past 20 min and my battery is at 72%).

I am saddened, to say the least, that such a great app has turned to be a piece of junk. It became part of my routine and now it is unusable. Time to move on, I guess.

I continued to use the app since my last review. I guess losing a 15-year history of dieting was too much to handle. Some updated corrected the sluggishness and battery drain.

title: MyFitnessPal should make their own Food Scale
text:
I’ve been using MyFitnessPal for so many years now, and it’s honestly amazing to see how much the app has grown. You guys are one of the OGs when it comes to tracking calories and nutrition.

One thing I’ve been thinking about is how cool it would be if MyFitnessPal came out with its own smart food scale. There are already some really good food scales out there that connect to calorie-tracking apps, and I feel like this is something MyFitnessPal could really take advantage of

Imagine having a food scale that connects directly to MyFitnessPal, where you can weigh your food and have the calories, protein, carbs, and fats automatically added to your food diary. It would make tracking so much easier.

I’ve also seen some really modern food scales with TFT color displays, and I think combining something like that with AI-powered features would be pretty cool. Especially if the scale could work with MyFitnessPal’s food database.

You guys already have such a huge community of people who use the app for their fitness and nutrition goals. I really think having your own food scale could be something worth looking into, and I wouldn’t be surprised if a lot of people would be interested in buying one.

Just an idea from someone who’s been using and appreciating the app for years. I would genuinely love to see you guys explore something like this

The good: intuitive interface, barcode scanning, easy meal logging, decent premium features.

The bad: unreliable nutrition database that undermines the entire purpose of the app. Even the "verified" entries aren't always accurate.

My advice: If you use this app, treat it as a rough estimate only. Always verify entries against the nutrition label on your food packaging before logging. If precision matters to you (like if you're following a specific diet for medical reasons), consider using the USDA FoodData Central directly or switching to an app with a more rigorous database like Cronometer.

It's frustrating because the app could be great if the data were trustworthy. Right now, you're putting in work to track accurately while fighting an inaccurate database.

text:
If you’re someone who actually exercises and wants an accurate net calorie number, this app is apparently not for you.
Seriously, this has to be one of the dumbest ways imaginable to track calories burned from exercise. I burn 600 calories working out, and Lose It tells me I burned 4. FOUR. Apparently my workout was basically a brisk walk to the refrigerator.
Instead of simply telling us how many calories we actually burned, Lose It uses some bizarre projected-burn system that makes the exercise numbers almost completely useless. I mean, who cares about some theoretical number? If I just burned 600 calories, I’d kind of like the app to acknowledge that fact.
And here’s the really fun part: how exactly are we supposed to know how much food we should eat if we don’t have an accurate net calorie number without doing a bunch of math? I hate math. That’s literally why I’m using an app.
This shouldn’t be complicated. Just give us a simple, accurate net calorie total for the day: calories consumed minus calories actually burned. If I eat 1,800 calories and burn 600 through exercise, I shouldn’t have to pull out a calculator, a spreadsheet, and possibly a degree in applied mathematics to figure out what my actual net calories are.
Please stop trying to outsmart something that should be incredibly simple. We exercise. We burn calories. Just count the stupid calories.

title: Expensive, Inaccurate, and Constantly Needs Correcting
text:
I paid for a yearly subscription to Cal AI and genuinely regret it. The entire point of using a nutrition-tracking app is to make tracking easier and more accurate, but I constantly have to double-check and correct this app.

Even when I scan the actual nutrition label, it frequently enters values that do not match the label right in front of me. I would estimate that 9 out of 10 products I scan require some kind of manual correction. At that point, what exactly is the AI saving me?

The Food Score is even more frustrating. The app repeatedly tells me that I am low on protein when my logged numbers clearly show that I have met or even exceeded the protein goal already set in the app. Foods can also receive poor scores because Cal AI fails to properly calculate things like fiber, sugar, and sodium. Worse, when I manually correct inaccurate nutrition information, the scoring system still does not seem to properly account for those corrections.

That makes the score feel arbitrary rather than useful. A nutrition app should not penalize a food because the app itself failed to capture its nutritional information correctly.

For a paid product—especially an annual subscription—basic nutrition-label scanning and macro calculations should be reliable. I should not have to audit nearly every entry against the package.

At this point, the only reason I continue using Cal AI is to maintain a rough idea of how many calories I am eating. I do not trust it enough for accurate macro or micronutrient tracking, and I definitely do not trust its Food Score.

I wish I had not purchased the yearly subscription. The concept is great, but the execution has been extremely disappointing.

title: Decent, Work Flow Needs Help - Update
text:
I've been using this app for over 6 months  now.   It's got some neat features, but a few problems.

In addition to the messed up work flow issues I detailed below, one of the built-in features just doesn’t work.  I cannot export my data.  

I have put in a ticket at least three times now.  Each time, I send them a screenshot and info on my device type/sw.   Then crickets.  I can live with all of the other issues, but being ignored by tech support is what’s causing me to downgrade this rating.  

This app recently sold for a *lot* of money.  You’d think with that kind of investment, they could put a few dollars into development.  

Here’s my comments from the 4 week mark:

The work flow is really poor.  For example, if you want to enter a recipe, you have to go to "Saved Foods" and then "My Meals".  This was not obvious the first time I tried it (nor does it not make sense.)

Then, if I want to create a recipe (or, "meal" as they call it) I can add something from "Saved Foods" or "My Foods".  It is not intuitively obvious what "My Foods" is for or how it differs from "Saved Foods."

If I want to add an item to a recipe that I physically have in front of me, I have to add it to "Saved Meals" first.  To add something to "Saved Meals", you apparently have to add it to your current meal, save it, then delete it.  Maybe there's another way,but again, not intuitively obvious.  

Another issue is serving size.  If I add an item to "Saved Foods", it doesn't put anywhere in the description or data what that serving size was.  So if I eat it at a later time, when I pull it up, I don't know what they considered as a serving size.  Yes, sometimes it lets me go in and put in a specific measure (oz, cups, etc.), but if say, the serving size was based on a number of pieces (let's say 6 for an example), then I add it to my day's intake but only ate say 3 pieces, there's no way to know that the nutrition was based on 6 pieces.  I work around this by editing the item name and putting the serving size in the description.  I shouldn't have to do this.  The information is obviously there.  Let us use it.

Finally, the "Saved Foods" list just grows and grows.  Yes, there is a search function, but you don't always hit the search term correctly, so you either have to try multiple times, or scroll through an ever growing long list.  It would be nice to be able to organize and sort this list so I can access it easily.

I'm sure there's things I haven't figured out yet, but it shouldn't be that way.  If something isn't intuitive, there needs to be instructions.  Just because the developers think their app works fine doesn't mean it does if you weren't in on developing it.  It's like this app never went through a real beta test, or else the developers don't really use it themselves.

This could be a good app, but like I said - work flow. It's not right,

title: FAMILY PLAN  INVITES - READ FIRST
text: READ FIRST BEFORE INVITING FAMILY -  If you are using Cal AI (The Calorie/Diet Tracker)If you bought the Cal AI Family Plan (usually around $59.99/year) through the Apple App Store or Google Play Store, the app itself does not manage the invitations. It relies entirely on Apple or Google’s built-in system.  The Trap: If you send an invite link from inside the app, it often just drops the other person onto a generic download or onboarding screen. Because the app aggressively pushes its own 3-day free trial during setup, your family member might unknowingly sign up for their own individual premium trial rather than linking to yours.  The Fix: Don't invite them through the app. Make sure they are added directly to your Apple Family Sharing or Google Family Group via your phone's main settings. Once they are part of your phone's official family group, they just need to download the app, and it should automatically recognize the shared subscription.
